question: Where do I find a fractional CRO in Savannah?
body:
## Direct Answer

You find a fractional CRO for a Savannah company through three practical channels: fractional-executive marketplaces and go-to-market talent networks that vet part-time revenue leaders, warm referrals from your local banking, investor, CPA, and founder circles, and targeted LinkedIn outreach filtered by title, geography, and industry fit. Expect to pay a monthly retainer for roughly one to three days a week rather than a full-time salary, and prioritize proven revenue-turnaround experience over physical proximity, because most fractional engagements run hybrid or fully remote with periodic onsite time.

Savannah's senior revenue-leadership pool is thinner than Atlanta's or Charlotte's, so the winning move is to widen your search radius to the broader Southeast and the Coastal Georgia corridor while keeping onsite cadence negotiable. A fractional Chief Revenue Officer gives a growing company senior go-to-market horsepower — sales, marketing, customer success, and RevOps alignment — without the full loaded cost of a permanent chief. The rest of this guide covers exactly where to look, how to vet candidates, what to expect on cost, and how to structure the engagement so it actually moves revenue. If you read only this section, here is the short version: define your mandate and budget first, source from vetted networks plus warm referrals, run a paid trial before a long commitment, and buy for fit and outcomes rather than for a local zip code.

## What is a fractional CRO, and when does a Savannah company actually need one?

A fractional CRO is a seasoned revenue executive who works with your company part-time — typically one to three days per week — owning the entire go-to-market engine across sales, marketing, and customer success. Unlike a consultant who advises and leaves, a fractional CRO carries a number, builds the operating rhythm, hires and coaches the team, and stays accountable for pipeline and bookings. They embed in your leadership meetings, sit in on live deals, and rebuild your forecasting and compensation plans — but they do it on a fraction of the time and cost of a full-time chief. The word "fractional" describes the time commitment, not the seniority: you are still buying a career revenue leader, just for the hours where their judgment compounds.

For a Savannah business, the trigger is usually one of a few recognizable moments. You have crossed roughly $1M to $10M in revenue and your founder-led selling has plateaued. You have reps but no repeatable process, or a marketing team generating leads that sales cannot convert. You are preparing for a raise or a sale and need clean revenue metrics and a defensible growth story. Or you have the budget for senior go-to-market leadership but not the deal flow to justify a permanent CRO salary plus equity. If any of those describe you, fractional leadership is the pragmatic bridge — you get strategic clarity now and can convert to full-time later once the model is proven.

The other honest reason Savannah founders choose fractional is local supply. The metro economy skews toward the port and logistics, manufacturing, tourism and hospitality, healthcare, and a growing but still-young tech and professional-services scene. Career revenue chiefs who have scaled SaaS or B2B services from single-digit millions to mid-eight-figure revenue are simply rarer here than in a major hub like Atlanta. Fractional engagements let you tap that talent from anywhere while keeping the option of periodic onsite time — which means your search should optimize for the right operator, not the closest one.

It is worth being clear about what a fractional CRO is *not*. They are not a warm body to make cold calls, not a marketing agency, and not a short-term "spray a playbook and leave" consultant. They are also not the right first hire for a company with no traction at all. The role earns its keep when there is a real revenue engine that is misfiring — leads that do not convert, a forecast nobody trusts, a comp plan that rewards the wrong behavior, or a founder who is still personally closing every deal. If that is your situation, a fractional CRO is one of the highest-leverage moves available to you.

## Where do I actually find fractional CRO candidates near Savannah?

Start with the channels that pre-filter for the exact profile you want, then layer in referral and direct outreach. The highest-signal sources are the fractional-executive marketplaces and revenue-talent networks — these platforms vet operators, publish track records, and match you to people who have done fractional work before. That last point matters, because running a fractional practice well is a distinct skill from being a great full-time CRO: it demands fast diagnosis, ruthless prioritization, and the discipline to install systems that outlast the engagement. Complement the marketplaces with your warm network, which in Savannah is unusually powerful because the business community is tight and referrals travel fast.

Here is the search flow that works, moving from broadest reach to most-targeted:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Define the mandate and budget] --> B[Fractional executive marketplaces]
    A --> C[Warm referrals from local network]
    A --> D[LinkedIn targeted outreach]
    B --> E[Shortlist three to five candidates]
    C --> E
    D --> E
    E --> F[Structured vetting and reference checks]
    F --> G[Paid trial engagement]
    G --> H[Full fractional retainer]
```

**Fractional and go-to-market talent networks.** National marketplaces and executive communities such as Chief Outsiders, Bolster, and the Pavilion community specialize in placing part-time and interim revenue and go-to-market executives. These are the fastest path to a vetted shortlist because they carry operators who already run fractional practices and can start within weeks. Filter by industry adjacency — SaaS, B2B services, logistics and supply-chain tech, manufacturing, healthcare — rather than by zip code. A revenue leader who has scaled a motion that looks like yours, from two states away, will almost always beat a local generalist.

**Warm referrals inside Coastal Georgia.** Ask the people who see revenue leaders in action: your commercial banker, your CPA and law firm, other founders in your space, and the regional ecosystem builders. The Savannah Economic Development Authority (SEDA), The Creative Coast, and the Savannah Area Chamber of Commerce all convene founders and operators and can point you toward fractional talent already working locally or regionally. A referral from someone who has watched a candidate deliver is worth more than any polished profile, because it comes with an implicit reference attached.

**LinkedIn targeted outreach.** Search titles directly — "Fractional CRO," "Fractional VP Sales," "Interim Chief Revenue Officer" — filtered to Savannah, Atlanta, Charleston, Jacksonville, and the broader Southeast. Many fractional operators explicitly list "Fractional" in their headline and openly take on new clients. A short, specific message describing your stage, revenue band, and the outcome you want tends to get strong response rates, because these operators are actively developing business and will recognize a serious buyer immediately.

Widening geographically is not a compromise — it is the point. Charleston and Jacksonville are each within a few hours' drive, Atlanta is a short flight or a manageable drive, and a strong operator who runs a monthly or quarterly onsite cadence will out-deliver a mediocre local hire every time. Treat proximity as a nice-to-have that lowers travel cost, not as a filter that shrinks your talent pool to whoever happens to live nearby.

## How do I vet a fractional CRO so I don't hire the wrong one?

Vetting a fractional revenue chief is different from vetting a full-time one, because you are buying focused impact on a clock, not a multi-year relationship. You want proof they can diagnose a revenue problem fast, install a system, and transfer that capability to your team so the engine keeps running when their days taper. Screen for pattern-matching, not résumé prestige — the real question is whether they have fixed a revenue problem shaped like yours, at your stage, in a comparable motion. A leader who scaled a $50M enterprise sales org may be the wrong fit for a $3M company that sells a self-serve product, and vice versa.

Anchor your evaluation on evidence, not vibes. Ask every candidate to walk you through a specific engagement: what the revenue looked like when they arrived, the two or three levers they pulled, the metrics that moved, and how long it took. Strong operators speak in specifics — pipeline coverage ratios, win-rate deltas, sales-cycle compression, net revenue retention — and they will tell you candidly what did not work. Then check references with operators who reported to them or hired them, and ask the one question that matters most: "Would you hire them again, and for what specifically?" The answer to the second half often reveals whether they are a builder, a fixer, or a maintainer.

Use this scorecard to compare candidates on the dimensions that predict fractional success:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Candidate] --> B[Stage fit at your revenue band]
    A --> C[Motion fit sales led or product led]
    A --> D[Documented revenue outcomes]
    A --> E[Systems and RevOps rigor]
    A --> F[Coaching and team transfer]
    A --> G[Fractional experience and availability]
    B --> H[Weighted fit score]
    C --> H
    D --> H
    E --> H
    F --> H
    G --> H
```

A few red flags to weed out early. Be wary of the candidate who only wants to sell strategy decks and will not touch the CRM, the comp plan, or the pipeline reviews — fractional CROs earn their retainer in the operating cadence, not the offsite. Be cautious of anyone who over-commits on days across many clients; a person spread across six retainers cannot give you real attention, and the diagnostic phase alone demands focus. Discount generic playbook talk that is not grounded in your specific motion, buyer, and price point. And be skeptical of anyone who promises a fixed revenue outcome before they have seen your CRM data — honest operators diagnose before they forecast.

## What does a fractional CRO cost in the Savannah market?

Fractional CRO pricing is structured as a monthly retainer tied to a committed number of days per week, and it varies widely by the operator's pedigree and the scope of the mandate. The honest answer is that rates are set by the individual and the market, not by a published fee schedule, so treat any single number you hear as a range to negotiate rather than a fixed price. What is consistent is the *shape* of the deal: a recurring monthly retainer, an initial term of roughly three to six months, and a scope that maps to a specific number of working days per week. Some operators also structure a portion of upside — a bonus tied to bookings or a small equity slice — but the core is almost always a predictable retainer.

The economics are the reason fractional works. A full-time CRO in a mid-market company commands a substantial base salary plus variable comp, equity, and benefits — an all-in cost that a sub-$10M company often cannot justify against its current deal flow. A fractional arrangement gives you a slice of that same caliber of leader for the days you actually need, which is why the model has spread quickly among growth-stage companies. You are paying for judgment and system-building concentrated into the hours that move the needle, and you can scale the commitment up or down as the business changes.

Structure the commercial terms to protect both sides. Define the mandate in writing — the outcomes, the cadence, the days per week, and what "done" looks like at 90 and 180 days. Start with a paid trial or a short initial term so both parties can confirm fit before committing to a longer runway. And clarify the endgame up front: many fractional engagements are explicitly designed to hand off to a full-time hire that the fractional CRO helps you recruit and onboard, so agree early on whether you are renting leadership indefinitely or bridging to a permanent seat. Getting this ambiguity out of the way prevents the awkward drift where neither side knows whether the relationship is ending or deepening.

Whatever the number, judge it against the cost of the status quo. A stalled sales team, a leaky funnel, and a founder buried in deals they should have delegated all carry a real price — in lost bookings, in slow decisions, and in the opportunity cost of a founder who cannot work *on* the business because they are stuck working *in* it. If a fractional CRO compresses your sales cycle, lifts win rates, and frees the founder to run the company, the retainer usually pays for itself well inside the initial term.

## How do I structure the engagement so it actually delivers?

The engagement design matters as much as the person. The best fractional CRO relationships share a common architecture: a short diagnostic phase, a prioritized fix list, an operating cadence the fractional leader owns, and a deliberate capability transfer to your team. Skip the diagnostic and you get generic playbooks; skip the transfer and revenue slides the moment the engagement ends. Build both in from day one, and write them into the agreement so they are commitments rather than good intentions.

Begin with a 30-day diagnostic. Give the fractional CRO access to your CRM, your last few quarters of pipeline and bookings, your comp plans, and your team, and ask for a written assessment: where the revenue is leaking, what the two or three highest-leverage fixes are, and what the 90-day plan looks like. This phase alone often surfaces problems founders have felt but could not name — misaligned incentives, a broken lead-to-opportunity handoff, a forecast that is closer to fiction than math. From there, the fractional CRO installs the operating rhythm: weekly pipeline reviews, a real forecast, a clean comp plan, and clear metrics that everyone reads the same way.

The cadence is where the value compounds. A good fractional CRO runs your revenue meetings, coaches your reps and managers in live deals, and holds the team accountable to the numbers — that consistency is what turns a plan into results. Insist on that operating discipline in the agreement, and insist on documentation: the playbooks, dashboards, and process docs the fractional leader creates should stay with you as company assets. The whole point is that when the engagement winds down or converts to full-time, the revenue engine keeps running because the *system* — not just the person — was installed. Treat every artifact they produce as intellectual property you are buying, and store it where the team can keep using it.

Finally, measure relentlessly against the plan you agreed to. Set leading and lagging indicators up front — pipeline coverage, win rate, sales-cycle length, bookings, and net revenue retention — and review them on a fixed cadence. If the metrics are not moving by the end of the first quarter and the diagnosis has not evolved to explain why, that is a signal to renegotiate scope or part ways. A strong fractional operator will welcome that accountability, because delivering measurable outcomes is exactly how they earn their next referral.

## FAQ

### What does CRO stand for, and how is it different from a sales consultant?

CRO stands for Chief Revenue Officer — the executive who owns the entire go-to-market engine across sales, marketing, and customer success, accountable for total revenue and growth. A consultant advises and hands you a report; a fractional CRO owns a revenue number, runs the operating cadence, coaches the team, and stays accountable for results part-time. You are buying execution and accountability, not just recommendations.

### Can a fractional CRO work fully remote for a Savannah company?

Yes. Most fractional engagements run hybrid or fully remote, with periodic onsite visits for kickoffs, quarterly planning, and key deals. Prioritize proven revenue-turnaround experience and motion fit over physical proximity — a great operator elsewhere who commits to a regular onsite cadence usually beats a mediocre local hire.

### How long does a typical fractional CRO engagement last?

Most run somewhere between three and twelve months, often structured as a three-to-six-month initial term with renewal. Many are explicitly designed to bridge to a full-time CRO whom the fractional leader helps you recruit and onboard, so the relationship has a natural endpoint built in.

### What size company should hire a fractional CRO?

Typically companies roughly in the $1M to $10M revenue range that have some traction but have outgrown founder-led selling and need a repeatable, scalable go-to-market system without the cost of a permanent chief. A pre-revenue startup is usually better served by a fractional VP of Sales or continued founder-led selling first, because there is not yet an engine to systematize.

### How is a fractional CRO different from a fractional VP of Sales?

A fractional CRO owns all revenue functions — sales, marketing, and customer success — and the cross-functional strategy that aligns them. A fractional VP of Sales owns the sales team and quota specifically. Choose the CRO when the whole go-to-market engine needs alignment; choose the VP of Sales when the sales motion itself is the primary gap.

### Where can I find fractional CROs if none are based in Savannah?

Widen your search to Atlanta, Charleston, Jacksonville, and the broader Southeast, and use national fractional-executive marketplaces and LinkedIn. Remote and hybrid engagements are standard, so a strong operator elsewhere with periodic onsite time is a completely viable option — and often the better one.

### How do I measure whether a fractional CRO is working?

Track leading and lagging revenue metrics agreed up front — pipeline coverage, win rate, sales-cycle length, bookings, and net revenue retention — reviewed against a 90-day plan. You should see process installed and metrics beginning to move within the first quarter, along with visible operating discipline like reliable forecasts and consistent pipeline reviews.

### Can a fractional CRO help me raise capital or prepare for a sale?

Yes. A common mandate is cleaning up revenue metrics, building a defensible forecast, and tightening the growth story ahead of a fundraise or exit, which materially strengthens how investors and acquirers evaluate the business. Just confirm the operator has done this specific work before, since diligence-ready reporting is its own discipline.
